turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I... I suppose I came in because things have just become completely untenable at work. As a chief executive, you expect a certain amount of behind-the-scenes chatter, you know, office politics, but this is... it's constant. I keep hearing people talking about me, specifically the board members and my senior staff. I'll be sitting in my private office trying to review our financials, and I can hear them right through the conference room walls, just going on and on about how I’m completely ruining the company. 

And the thing is, it's not just the walls. It comes through my phone, too. At first, I thought maybe a conference line was left connected or someone's mic was hot, so I started turning the device completely off. Powering it down entirely, putting it face down on the desk. But I still hear them coming through the speaker, even when the power is off, telling me I'm destroying everything we've built. 

It’s so incredibly clear, the voices are just so distinct and real, that I actually answer them back. I'll sit there and defend my strategic decisions out loud, telling them why they're wrong, and I'll be halfway through a sentence before I look around and realize... no one else is in the room. No one else heard it. But I hear it all day, Doctor, they just will not stop talking about me.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing distinct voices of board members and staff criticizing him through walls and a powered-off phone, which he responds to out loud, clearly indicating auditory hallucinations.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing these auditory experiences?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... I suppose it has been about three months now. Yes, it would be exactly three months, because I remember it started just as we were finalizing our end-of-quarter projections. I was sitting at my desk late one evening, trying to focus on the spreadsheets, and that was the very first time I noticed the voices coming through the drywall. At the time, I just assumed the senior staff were working late and being incredibly unprofessional in the adjacent room. I almost buzzed my assistant to tell them to keep the noise down. 

But it never stopped after that night. Day after day, week after week, it just kept happening. And then the phone situation started a few weeks into it. So for a whole business quarter now, an entire three months, I have been dealing with this. Ninety days of constant scrutiny, of powering down my phone and still hearing them mock my leadership through the dead speaker. It is just exhausting, Doctor, to live like this for three months straight, having to defend myself to an empty room because they just will not leave me be.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing voices coming through the drywall and from a powered-down phone, which are clear auditory hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: During these past three months, have you experienced any significant periods where your mood felt unusually high, energetic, or conversely, extremely low and hopeless?
turns.patient_response:
High or energetic? Well, I... I mean, as a chief executive, you obviously have to maintain a certain baseline of energy and drive. You simply don't get to the C-suite by being sluggish or lacking vision. But unusually high? No, no, not at all. I certainly haven't been bouncing off the walls or staying up for days on end with wild ideas, if that's what you're getting at. I've just been trying to keep the company on track while dealing with all of this constant interference. 

And as for feeling extremely low or hopeless... I really wouldn't use those words. Frustrated? Absolutely. I am beyond frustrated. When you're sitting in your own private office, trying to do your job, and your own phone is criticizing your Q3 strategy even when the screen is black and it's completely powered down... you feel exasperated. You feel angry, you feel completely targeted by your own staff. But hopeless? No, I'm not sitting in bed crying all day or giving up on the company. 

I still get up at 5:30 AM every single morning, just like I have for the last fifteen years. I do my forty-five minutes on the elliptical, I drink my double espresso, and I go straight to the office. I haven't missed a single executive committee meeting in all these months, despite the whispering. So, my mood is... well, it's just my normal mood, really. I'm just under an incredible, crushing amount of unwarranted scrutiny from these people. It’s the circumstances that are so completely unacceptable, Doctor, not my mood. I just need them to stop talking about me so I can actually focus on my work.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the voices you hear, have you noticed any other unusual experiences, such as feeling as though your thoughts are being broadcast out loud for others to hear or that someone is putting thoughts into your mind that aren't your own?
turns.patient_response:
Broadcast out loud? No, no, absolutely not. I mean... just think about the position I hold, Doctor. If my thoughts were somehow being broadcast out loud for anyone to hear, the market would be in absolute chaos by now. I hold highly confidential, market-moving data in my head every single day. Mergers and acquisitions, proprietary algorithms, quarterly guidance weeks before we release it to the SEC... if people could just hear what I was thinking, we would have insider trading scandals left and right. So no, my thoughts are entirely private. Thank goodness. 

And as for someone putting thoughts into my mind... well, honestly, I find that just a little bit insulting. I didn't get to the C-suite by letting other people do my thinking for me. My strategic vision is entirely my own. I spend hours—sometimes I'll sit in my home office from eight in the evening until well past midnight, just me, a legal pad, and a glass of sparkling water, meticulously charting out our five-year growth trajectories. Nobody is putting those ideas there. They are mine. I am a remarkably independent thinker. Always have been, ever since I was taking night classes and trying to get my footing in the business world. I trust my own mind completely.

The problem isn't my mind, Doctor. My mind is perfectly secure, it is as sharp as it has ever been. The problem is what's happening outside of it. It's the physical reality of the board members and... and the VP of Operations—I know it's him, I recognize his exact tenor and that condescending little throat-clearing thing he does—literally speaking about me through the drywall. That's what you need to understand, that's what we need to focus on. I don't have magical thoughts floating around or people controlling my brain. I have an insubordinate, toxic executive team that is using... I don't know, acoustic technology or just blatant, screaming disrespect, to harass me through a powered-down smartphone. That is the issue here. I don't understand why we're talking about my thoughts when the real, tangible problem is what my staff is saying about me right out in the open.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that his executive team is harassing him using acoustic technology through a powered-down smartphone.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing the voice of the VP of Operations speaking about him through the drywall and a powered-down phone, indicating auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies any cognitive decline, stating his mind is 'perfectly secure' and 'as sharp as it has ever been.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to keep up with your daily hygiene, or have you found yourself feeling less interested in socializing or doing things you used to enjoy outside of work?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hygiene, no. I mean, I still shower, I still dress appropriately for the office. You can't show up to the executive suite looking disheveled, that would just give them more ammunition. I have my dry cleaning delivered every Tuesday and Thursday, just like always. I still wear my usual suits, I make sure my hair is presentable. So that hasn't changed. 

But... socializing? Enjoying things? That is... that's a different story entirely, Doctor. I really don't know how to explain it without sounding like I'm not doing my job, but... I just don't care anymore. And that is so unlike me. I used to be the one driving every single idea in the boardroom. I was the one calling people after openings, organizing the charity galas, making sure every executive retreat was perfectly planned down to the last detail. I loved it. I absolutely thrived on it. It was my life. 

Now? Now I can sit at my desk in my office for hours—literally hours, Doctor—just staring at the meeting agenda. I'll have the paper right in front of me, and I just... I don't feel anything. I don't feel that drive, that spark, that passion I used to have for the work. I just sit there. And it's the same at home. I barely speak to my husband these days. He'll ask me about my day, and I just don't have the energy or the desire to string the words together to tell him. I just give him a one-word answer and go to my study. 

And my staff... I barely speak to them either, unless it's absolutely, strictly necessary for a critical decision. I used to walk the floor, you know? I used to chat with the department heads, get a feel for the morale, really engage with the people building this company. Now I just keep my door closed. I just want to be left alone. I don't want to go to the networking dinners, I don't want to play golf on the weekends, I don't even want to read the industry magazines I used to devour. It's just this... this massive emptiness where my ambition used to be. I feel almost nothing about the work I used to love so much. I just sit there, staring at the agenda, waiting for the day to end so I can go home and sit in silence. It's like someone just turned the volume down on my entire personality, except for the parts of me that have to deal with those voices. That's the only thing that gets any reaction out of me anymore. Everything else is just... flat.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient mentions having to 'deal with those voices,' indicating the presence of auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes multiple negative symptoms, including avolition (sitting for hours staring), alogia (barely speaking to husband or staff), asociality (keeping the door closed, wanting to be left alone), and diminished emotional expression (feeling 'flat').
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes experiencing a 'massive emptiness' and emotional numbness, stating they 'feel almost nothing' and that everything is 'flat.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly reports a complete loss of interest and pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, such as their work, playing golf, and reading industry magazines.

turns.doctor_question: During these three months where you have felt this loss of interest and drive, have you also noticed any physical changes, such as a significant shift in your appetite or your ability to get a restful night's sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Appetite or sleep? No, not really. I mean, my routine is exactly the same as it has always been. My assistant, Sarah—she's been with me for six years now, she knows my schedule down to the absolute minute—she still orders my usual lunch from the bistro down the street. It's always a grilled chicken salad with the dressing on the side on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and maybe a light turkey wrap on Mondays and Wednesdays. I eat it at my desk while I'm looking over the afternoon briefs. I don't really think about it, I just eat it because it's there and I know the human body requires fuel. It's not about enjoying the food anymore, it's just... maintenance, really. And dinners, well, my husband usually cooks or we order in, and I eat my normal portion. I haven't been starving myself or stress-eating, if that's what you mean. I've always been very disciplined about my diet, very structured. You have to be, when you're managing hundreds of employees and dealing with the constant whispering and the absolute lack of respect from the board. 

And sleep... no, my sleep is exactly the same, too. I am a creature of absolute habit, Doctor. I am in bed by 11:00 PM every single night. I read for exactly twenty minutes—usually a biography or some historical non-fiction, though lately, like I said, I haven't really been absorbing the words, I just turn the pages because that's what my nighttime routine dictates—and then I turn out the light. I sleep until my alarm goes off at 5:30 AM. Six hours and ten minutes, give or take. I don't toss and turn, I don't wake up in the middle of the night in a cold sweat. It's just... sleep. It's just another block of time on my calendar that I have to get through. 

The only thing that ever threatens my peace is when I'm in my study right before bed and I can hear the VP of Operations making those snide, passive-aggressive comments through the floorboards. But once I'm actually in bed and the white noise machine is on? I sleep just fine. I just wake up feeling... well, feeling that same heavy, flat emptiness I told you about. The physical mechanics of eating and sleeping are perfectly intact, Doctor. I'm maintaining the machine. It's just the... the point of it all, the drive behind it, that seems to have completely vanished.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing a coworker making comments through the floorboards of her study at home, indicating auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient reports waking up feeling a 'heavy, flat emptiness'.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient notes she no longer enjoys food and that her overall drive has 'completely vanished'.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient mentions she has not been absorbing the words while reading, indicating reduced concentration.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over your entire life, not just these past three months, have there been any other times where you heard voices or held beliefs that others didn't share, even when you weren't feeling this sense of emptiness or lack of drive?
turns.patient_response:
My entire life? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, you have to understand my background, Doctor. I didn't get handed a C-suite position on a silver platter. I only have a few years of college—I had to drop out and work my way up from the absolute bottom, outmaneuvering people with Ivy League MBAs at every single turn just to get a seat at the table. You do not survive that kind of ruthless corporate climb, and you certainly do not become a Chief Executive at forty-three, if you are walking around holding beliefs that aren't grounded in absolute, verifiable reality. My entire career has been built on seeing things exactly as they are. Data, market trends, profit margins, risk assessments. I have never had "unusual beliefs," as you call them, and I certainly have never heard voices before this current situation. 

This whole ordeal... the voices coming through the walls, the condescending comments coming out of my phone when the screen is completely black and powered down... that has only been happening for about the past three months. Exactly three months, actually, if I really look back at the calendar. It started right around the time we were locking in the Q3 projections. I remember it so vividly. I was in my office, reviewing the quarterly expenditures, and that was the very first time I heard the VP of Operations mocking my budget allocations right through the drywall. 

So no, this is not some lifelong issue. I have never experienced anything even remotely like this before. It is a very recent, very specific campaign of insubordination that started three months ago. Before that, my staff wouldn't have dared speak to me that way, let alone use whatever acoustic technology they are using to pipe their disrespect into my home study. So I really need you to understand that this is an isolated, three-month problem with a toxic executive team, not some historical defect in my character or my mind. My track record is flawless. It's just these last three months that have become a complete nightmare because of them.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that his executive team is using 'acoustic technology' to pipe disrespectful comments into his home study.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient clearly describes experiencing auditory hallucinations, specifically hearing voices coming through the walls and from a powered-down phone.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at that exact three-month mark, did the feelings of emptiness and loss of drive start at the exact same time you first heard the voices, or did one of those things begin before the other?
turns.patient_response:
No... no, they didn't start at the same time at all. I know I was just talking about the three-month mark for the... the insubordination, the comments coming through the floorboards and the phone. But the emptiness? That absolute loss of drive and passion I was describing? 

That has actually been building for much, much longer. If I'm being perfectly precise, it's been about two years and four months. Yes, two years and four months exactly, because that was right when the board pushed through the big company expansion. They decided we needed to aggressively diversify our portfolio, so they created this massive new arts-and-commerce division. And, naturally, who do you think they put in charge of it? Me, of course. They always put me in charge when there's heavy lifting to be done, because they know I'll outwork everyone else in the building, Ivy League degree or not. 

I remember the sheer logistical nightmare of it like it was yesterday. Merging fine arts acquisitions with our standard commercial retail streams... it was endless. The vendor negotiations, the endless strategy meetings, the absolute bureaucratic maze of getting the galleries and the retail spaces integrated. I was working eighty, sometimes ninety-hour weeks to make sure that division launched flawlessly. And it did launch flawlessly, Doctor. It was a complete triumph on paper. We exceeded our first-quarter projections by eighteen percent. 

But right around then... right in the thick of that expansion two years and four months ago, that's when I first noticed it. That tiny crack in my enthusiasm. I thought I was just exhausted from the launch, you know? I thought, 'I just need a weekend off, I just need to sleep in on a Sunday.' But it didn't go away. It just kept building. Month after month, for over two years, that spark just kept fading. It started with me skipping a networking dinner here and there, and then it became dreading the quarterly reviews, until it just turned into this massive, heavy void where my ambition used to live. 

So the emptiness was already there. It had been slowly hollowing me out for over two years. It wasn't until three months ago that my executive team decided to start taking advantage of it with their whispering campaigns and their technological tricks. The voices are recent, Doctor. But the loss of my drive? That started the second they handed me the arts-and-commerce division two years and four months ago.

turns.doctor_question: Have you found that your thoughts have become jumbled, or that you have difficulty following a conversation or keeping your train of thought while you are working?
turns.patient_response:
Jumbled? No. No, not at all. If my thoughts were jumbled, Doctor, I wouldn't last five minutes in my office. 

I mean, you have to understand the sheer volume of information I process on a daily basis. Just... just take yesterday morning, for example. Or maybe it was Tuesday, but regardless, I had a back-to-back review of the Q4 supply chain logistics. It's an absolute nightmare right now with all the overseas shipping delays, the tariff fluctuations we're dealing with, and the domestic warehousing bottlenecks. I sat at the head of that conference table for three solid hours, tracking every single metric, every single excuse the logistics team tried to throw at me to justify their bloated overhead. I didn't lose my train of thought once. I cross-referenced their current expenditure reports with the projections we made back in January entirely from memory. 

So I can follow a conversation perfectly. In fact, I probably follow it better than the people I'm talking to. I have to listen to what they're saying, what they're *not* saying, the little micro-expressions they make when they think I'm looking down at my tablet. Because, like I said, they are just waiting for me to show weakness. The VP of Operations, the board... if I started losing my train of thought, if I started rambling or looking confused, they would pounce on it in a heartbeat. They would use it as leverage to push me out and replace me with one of their Ivy League friends. 

My mind is completely clear. It's... it's actually the one thing I can still absolutely rely on. Even with this massive, heavy void sitting in my chest that makes everything feel pointless, and even with the constant, ridiculous insults they pipe into my room to try and distract me... my cognitive function is immaculate. I read the briefs, I synthesize the data, I issue the directives. There is no fog in my head, Doctor. Everything is perfectly, almost painfully, clear. I know exactly what is going on at all times, and I never lose the thread of what I'm doing.
